extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for analyzing whether an invention is anticipated under 35 U.S.C. §102, focusing on printed publication/prior-publication, the on-sale bar, and inherent anticipation. Summarizes legal tests, evidentiary considerations, and recent Federal Circuit decisions that shape those standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory timing for prior art (35 U.S.C. §102(a)/(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is barred from patentability if anticipated by art that was publicly disclosed prior to the applicant’s date of invention (35 U.S.C. §102(a)) or if publicly disclosed more than one year before the U.S. filing date (35 U.S.C. §102(b)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing is crucial; determine the relevant critical date for the inventor and the one-year grace period for U.S. filings. Use these dates as the baseline for evaluating whether a reference qualifies as prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: What constitutes 'public disclosure' for anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Public disclosure encompasses certain kinds of knowledge, use, publication, description, and sale that make the invention available to the public as prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the prior act conveyed the invention to the public in a way that would enable persons of ordinary skill to practice the claimed invention. Public disclosure can occur via publications, sales, uses, or other disseminations of information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed publication requirement (Klopfenstein four-factor framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior reference qualifies as a 'printed publication' based on fact-specific evidence of public accessibility, using factors such as length of time available, expertise of the target audience, expectations about copying, and ease of copying.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the four Klopfenstein factors: (1) length of time the reference was available; (2) expertise/sophistication of the intended audience; (3) reasonable expectations (or lack) that the reference would not be copied; and (4) ease of copying. Also consider traditional indicia (indexed/catalogued, actively distributed to the field). Recent cases (e.g., Klopfenstein, SRI Int’l v. ISS, Application of Bayer) show these factors are weighed together; obscurity of location (e.g., obscure file name or hidden directory) can defeat a finding of a printed publication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accessibility analysis for online postings (FTP/Internet) as printed publications
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination whether materials posted online (FTP, web pages, conference postings) are printed publications depends on how readily persons of ordinary skill could locate and access the material, and whether indexing or guidance was required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compare online postings to physical analogues (e.g., conference posters vs. unshelved theses). Consider whether the directory structure or metadata made the item findable, whether the link/address was broadly disseminated or only provided to select individuals, and whether copying was simple. Cases: SRI Int’l (FTP posting found not to be a printed publication when filename/location was obscure) and Klopfenstein (conference posters were publications).

rubrics_metrics.name: On-sale bar (Pfaff two-part test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Pfaff v. Wells Electronics, an invention is barred if (1) there was a commercial offer for sale before the critical date, and (2) the invention was ready for patenting at the time of the offer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate both prongs: evidence of a commercial sale/offer (not merely informational or promotional activity) and whether the invention had been reduced to practice or was otherwise 'ready for patenting' (e.g., workable prototype, enabling disclosure). Examine documents, prototypes, communications, and admissions about readiness and commercialization. Case examples: Pfaff; Atlanta Attachment Co. v. Leggett & Platt; In re Cygnus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental-use exception to the on-sale bar (primary-purpose test & reduction-to-practice limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental use can exempt pre-critical-date transfers from the on-sale bar if the primary purpose of the transaction was experimentation (not commercial exploitation); however, the exception is narrow and limited by whether the invention has been reduced to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the 'primary purpose' of the transaction—was it to experiment and perfect the invention or was it commercial? The exception is constrained once an invention is reduced to practice: many Federal Circuit decisions hold that experimentation generally cannot excuse on-sale activity after reduction to practice. Profit is not required to find commercialization; oral confidentiality agreements may be insufficient. Cases: Atlanta Attachment (primary-purpose analysis; experimental use fails if commercial interests predominate), In re Cygnus (beta testing held commercial where inventor had reduced to practice).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherent anticipation standard (necessity of inherently present limitations)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is inherently anticipated if every element is either expressly or inherently present in a single prior-art reference; inherency requires that the missing limitation is necessarily present in the reference, not merely possibly or conjecturally present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove inherency with clear evidence that the unstated limitation necessarily follows from the prior art as would be recognized by persons of ordinary skill. Expert testing/demonstrations that reliably reproduce the inherent result are persuasive; mere conjecture or speculation is insufficient. Patentee failure to rebut repeatable testing evidence can support a finding of inherency. Case: In re Omeprazole (majority finding inherency based on consistent expert re-creation; dissent emphasized 'necessarily present' standard).
